phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ] followed by high front vowel [i], Tone 1 (high level, ˥). Pinyin 'x' has no English equivalent; it is the 'sh' of 'she' pushed forward toward the teeth.
Labial-velar approximant [w] with the final [aŋ] (open central vowel + velar nasal), Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥).
Bilabial nasal [m] with high back rounded vowel [u], Tone 3 (dipping, ˨˩˦) — the low, dipping contour that falls before it rises.

pronunciation.approximation: shee-WAHNG-moo — Xī held high and level like a sustained note, wáng rising from mid to high as in a question, mǔ dipping low and turning up again.

pronunciation.note: 西王母 means 'Queen Mother of the West' — xī (west), wáng (king, sovereign), mǔ (mother). The Modern Standard Mandarin reading is Xīwángmǔ (Tones 1-2-3), as recorded in the Unihan Database (Unicode Consortium, kMandarin) and standard Mandarin dictionaries. The tone-marked Pinyin restoration Xīwángmǔ preserves the citation tones of all three syllables; in connected speech the third tone on mǔ is often realized as a low half-third tone, but the lexical tone remains Tone 3.

domains.title: The Western Paradise
domains.subtitle: The Peaches of Immortality, Mount Kūnlún, and the Taming of a Wilderness Goddess
domains.lead: Xīwángmǔ, the Queen Mother of the West, has the strangest biography of any great Chinese goddess: in the oldest text she is a tiger-toothed power of plague on Mount Kūnlún; by the Han she is enthroned in the western paradise; by the Tang she hosts the Peach Banquet and guards the elixir. The wilderness was never banished from her — it was enthroned.

cards.name: Mount Kūnlún
cards.desc: Her paradise stands on Mount Kūnlún at the western edge of the world, the axis where heaven leans down to meet the wild earth.

cards.name: The Peaches of Immortality
cards.desc: The pántáo ripen once every three thousand years; to taste one is to step outside death's jurisdiction — which is why the Monkey King could not resist them.

cards.name: Tiger's Teeth, Leopard's Tail
cards.desc: Her archaic form keeps its claws: the Shān Hǎi Jīng gives her a tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail, the regalia of a mistress of plague and calamity.

cards.name: Sovereign of Yin and the West
cards.desc: In mature Taoist theology she rules yin, the west, and all goddesses, balanced against Dōngwánggōng's yang and east — the two poles of a complete cosmos.

symbols.name: The shèng headdress
symbols.meaning: Her ancient insignia of authority — the distinctive headdress she wears even in her oldest, wildest images

symbols.name: Tiger's teeth and leopard's tail
symbols.meaning: The zoomorphic vestiges of her primordial form, marking her dominion over plague and calamity

symbols.name: The Peaches of Immortality
symbols.meaning: Sovereignty over death itself — fruit that ripens once in three thousand years and frees the eater from mortality

symbols.name: Mount Kūnlún
symbols.meaning: The western paradise at the edge of the world, where her palace and orchards stand

symbols.name: The tallies
symbols.meaning: The tokens her Han-era devotees carried from commandery to commandery as pledges of her protection and long life

mythology.lead: Xīwángmǔ's myths trace an arc no other Chinese deity matches: from wilderness terror to the most gracious sovereign of the Taoist heavens. Each age kept something of the last, so that the serene hostess of the Peach Banquet still carries the teeth and tail of the mountain power she once was.

myths.title: The Fearsome Portrait
myths.text: Her oldest portrait is the strangest. In the Classic of Mountains and Seas, compiled from Warring States to Han materials, the Queen Mother "has the form of a human, the tail of a leopard, the teeth of a tiger, and is good at whistling; her tangled hair is bound with a sheng headdress" (ch. 2, Xishan jing). A later stratum adds her office — she "presides over the calamities of heaven and the five punishments" (ch. 16, Dahuang xi jing), seated on Mount Kūnlún with three azure birds to fetch her food. She is not yet a queen in any courtly sense. She is the numinous danger of the far west itself: the lands where the sun goes down, source of plague and of everything the settled world cannot control. Later ages would dress her in silk and seat her among goddesses — but the earliest text keeps her wild, and the wildness never entirely left the throne.

myths.title: The Elixir for Hòuyì
myths.text: It is from Xīwángmǔ that immortality flows. The Huainanzi records that Hòuyì, the archer who shot down the nine excess suns, "begged the elixir of undying from the Queen Mother of the West" — and that his wife Héng'é stole it and fled to the moon, where she became the moon's goddess (her name later softened to Cháng'é under a Han emperor's name-taboo). Versions disagree about the theft — greed, fear, or rescue of the elixir from unworthy hands — but they agree on the source: no one in the Chinese cosmos rises beyond death except through the Queen Mother's treasury. The same storehouse reappears in every later system: her peaches ripen once in three thousand years; her banquet seats the assembled immortals; her garden is raided in every retelling of the Monkey King. Sovereignty over the boundary between life and death was her first office and remained her last — whether she wore a leopard's tail or a phoenix crown.

myths.title: The Movement of 3 BCE
myths.text: The Queen Mother was never only a goddess of mirrors and palace ladies. In 3 BCE — recorded in the Book of Han (ch. 11, Annals of Emperor Ai) — her cult ignited across the empire: crowds in more than twenty commanderies passed her tally-tokens (chóu) from hand to hand, sang and danced in the streets, wore her tokens, and converged on the capitals "thousands strung together", awaiting the fulfilment of her promise. The movement alarmed the court enough to be entered in the dynastic history — one of the earliest documented popular religious movements in China, three centuries before the organized Daoist church. The tallies were small pieces of wood, and their passing was the whole theology: a pledge, from the goddess of the west, that the world as it was could not last. The chroniclers record the phenomenon and not the promise. The crowds, clearly, knew what they were waiting for.

myths.title: The Theft of the Peaches
myths.text: Once in three thousand years the Peaches of Immortality ripen in the Queen Mother's orchard, and once in three thousand years she hosts the pántáohuì, the Peach Banquet, for the assembled immortals, gods, and buddhas of the three religions. In Journey to the West (ch. 5) the task of guarding the orchard is given, with fatal optimism, to Sūn Wùkōng — who samples the fruit systematically, dining on the 3,000-year, 6,000-year, and 9,000-year trees alike, and then crashes the feast itself in a disguise borrowed from a serving goddess. It is one of literature's great heists, and its comedy rests on real theology: the peaches are the most tightly held treasure in heaven, ripening on a schedule longer than recorded history, and the Queen Mother is their unanswerable custodian. The Monkey King's appetite did what no god could. It made her orchard — and her three-thousand-year patience — the most famous garden in Chinese fiction.

myths.title: The Hostess at the Jasper Pool
myths.text: Before she was a Taoist sovereign she was a royal hostess. The Mu Tianzi Zhuan (Account of King Mu) — a Warring States text unearthed in 281 CE from a Wei royal tomb — sends King Mu of Zhou to her Jasper Pool (Yáochí) at the western edge of the world. There she receives the traveling king as an equal: she sings to him in the text's archaic verse — "white clouds in the sky, the road long, mountains between us; may you not die, and come again" — and he answers in kind before turning his eight-horse team east. The scene is her earliest humane portrait, and it fixed two things: the title by which Taiwanese temples still know her, Golden Mother of the Jasper Pool, and her oldest character — not empress, not bureaucrat, but the hostess at the end of the road, inviting the greatest traveler of the age to live long enough to come back. Every later banquet descends from that first cup of wine at the edge of the world.

lore.syncretism: The Queen Mother travelled with Chinese letters and liturgy across East Asia. In Japan she is read Seiōbo, appearing in painting, garden imagery, and the literary imagination as the hostess of the western orchard; in Korea she is Seowangmo, present in folklore and shamanic song; in Vietnamese she is Tây Vương Mẫu, her name borne into the southern reception of the Taoist pantheon. Within China her deepest transformation was her absorption into organized Taoism, where she rose to the summit of the celestial hierarchy as sovereign of yin and the west, paired with Dōngwánggōng, the King Father of the East, as the balanced poles of the cosmos. Buddhist storytellers did not so much absorb her as borrow her orchard: the immortality peaches and the great banquet pass freely between Taoist and popular-Buddhist narrative worlds, and it is in that shared space that the Journey to the West stages her most famous scene.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Queen Mother never retired from the heavens. In Taoist temples across Taiwan and the diaspora she is venerated still, often under the title Golden Mother of the Jasper Pool, and her birthday is kept with festival observance. In art she rides phoenixes and cranes through centuries of painting, lacquer, and embroidery, and the immortal peach she tends became the standard emblem of longevity, pressed into birthday buns and painted onto porcelain as a wish for long life. The Journey to the West made her banquet immortal in another sense: every screen adaptation of the Monkey King's career — film, television, animation, games — must sooner or later raid her orchard. She remains what she has been since the Han mirrors first invoked her for blessing: the great goddess at the western edge of the world, holding the one treasure every mortal wants and no one may take uninvited.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Xīwángmǔ teaches that civilization does not destroy its wilderness; it enthrones it. The tiger-toothed power of the Shān Hǎi Jīng was not replaced by the serene hostess of the Peach Banquet — she was carried forward, wildness and all, into the highest seat of the Taoist heavens. The goddess who once sent plague became the goddess who grants endless life, and the two offices are not as far apart as they seem: both are sovereignty over the boundary between life and death, held by the same unanswerable hand.

To name a domain Xīwángmǔ is to claim that whole arc — the west where the sun descends, the orchard where three thousand years ripen into a single fruit, and the promise whispered from tally to tally through the Han commanderies: that mortality is a border, and someone keeps the gate.

lore.archaeology: The Queen Mother's earliest textual portrait is in the Classic of Mountains and Seas, compiled from Warring States through Han materials (roughly 4th–1st centuries BCE), where she appears with tiger's teeth and a leopard's tail on Mount Kūnlún. Her great material flourishing is Han: bronze mirrors invoke her by name for blessing and long life, and tomb reliefs and murals — most famously the Wu Liang shrine of the 2nd century CE — show her enthroned in the west, increasingly paired with Dōngwánggōng in the east. The Book of Han preserves the documentary trace of her popular cult in the millenarian movement of 3 BCE, when her tallies passed through the commanderies. By the medieval period, Taoist scriptures and liturgical texts had raised her to the summit of the goddess hierarchy, the form in which she has been worshipped ever since.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 西王母, written identically in traditional and simplified characters — none of the three graphs was altered in the twentieth-century simplification. Pinyin Xīwángmǔ (Tones 1-2-3) is the Modern Standard Mandarin reading, recorded in the Unihan Database and standard dictionaries: xī (west, Tone 1), wáng (sovereign, Tone 2), mǔ (mother, Tone 3). The registrable Unicode restoration uses the tone-marked Pinyin rather than the hanzi because PUNICODEX renders the original characters in the temple's 'Original Script' card while keeping the domain label pronounceable and internationally registrable; the tone marks ī, á, and ǔ carry the citation tones that plain ASCII drops.
